nameStory: One look at this mole's nose and you'll instantly understand its name! The star-nosed mole sports a bizarre fleshy nose with 22 finger-like tentacles radiating outward like a pink, wiggling star. This otherworldly facial feature is so distinctive that early naturalists couldn't think of anything else to call it.
description: The star-nosed mole is a hamster-sized underground mammal with one of the most unusual noses in the animal kingdom. Its most striking feature is a fleshy, star-shaped nose surrounded by 22 pink, finger-like tentacles that constantly wiggle and probe. The body is covered in dark, velvety fur, and like other moles, it has large front paws perfect for digging. This small mammal is about the size of a mouse but chunkier, weighing roughly as much as two golf balls.

idTips.label: Star Nose
idTips.description: The unmistakable fleshy pink star around the nose with 22 wiggling tentacles - no other animal in New England has anything like this bizarre facial feature

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Hamster-sized body with a chunky, cylindrical shape and enormous front paws that look like tiny shovels with long claws

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, velvety black or dark brown fur that feels like velvet and repels water - stroke it and it springs right back into place

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found near or in water, swimming with quick movements and diving underwater to hunt - unusual for a mole

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny hand-like front prints with long claw marks, often found in mud near water sources or wetland edges

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Prefers wet, marshy areas rather than dry lawns - look for tunnel openings near streams, wet meadows, and boggy soil

habitat: Star-nosed moles thrive in wet, marshy areas throughout New England, preferring moist, low-elevation spots near streams, ponds, and boggy meadows. Unlike other moles that stick to drier soils, these unusual mammals need wet or waterlogged ground where they can easily tunnel and hunt both underground and underwater. You'll find them in wetland edges, marshy fields, and along muddy streambanks where the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil thaws and becomes workable again. Fresh tunnel systems and muddy tracks appear near wetland edges as they resume intensive foraging.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with visible tunnel networks in wet meadows. Occasionally spotted swimming in shallow water during early morning or evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Continue active tunneling as they prepare for winter. Fresh molehills and tunnel openings remain visible in marshy areas throughout the season.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under snow and ice, creating tunnel systems in unfrozen marsh edges. Rarely seen but tunnel activity continues in areas where soil doesn't freeze solid.

funFact: The star-nosed mole is officially the world's fastest-eating mammal, able to identify and gobble up a tiny worm in just 120 milliseconds - that's faster than you can blink your eyes!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other mole species, but the star-shaped nose makes identification foolproof - no other mammal in North America has anything remotely similar. If you can see the nose clearly, you've definitely found a star-nosed mole.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a mole, star-nosed moles are actually semi-aquatic and excellent swimmers, which surprises many people who think of moles as strictly underground creatures. They're also not blind like other mole species are often thought to be.
compareHints: The star-nosed mole is the only member of its genus, making it truly unique. Compared to other New England moles like the eastern mole, it's much more aquatic in lifestyle and has that unmistakable star-shaped nose appendage. While other moles have sensitive snouts, none have the elaborate 22-tentacle nose structure that makes this species instantly recognizable.
